title: Count numbers with no two adjacent equal digits
prompt: Write countNoAdjacentEqual(n string) int returning how many integers in [1, n] have no two adjacent equal decimal digits, with n given as a decimal string of up to 19 digits. 11 and 100 are out, 121 and 10 are in. The tests go up to 10^18, so counting one number at a time is not an option: the work has to be per digit position, not per number.
explanation: Every digit DP is the same decomposition: split the numbers below the bound by the position where they first drop below it. Up to that position the prefix is exactly the bound's own prefix (the 'tight' prefix); at that position you place something strictly smaller; after it every position is free. The count of free completions depends only on how many positions are left and on the last digit placed, which here is 9^k because each digit only has to differ from the one before it. Two details do all the damage. The first is leading zeros: a 5 is not 0000000000000000005, so a shorter number must be counted as a shorter number, which is what the separate loop over digit lengths does (9 choices for the first digit, 9 for each after it). Writing the recursion without a 'have I started' flag silently rejects every number with fewer digits than the bound that begins with a repeat of a zero. The second is that walking further along the tight prefix is only legal while that prefix is itself valid: once the bound has two equal adjacent digits, nothing tight can be extended, and the loop has to stop rather than keep adding free completions. The recursive form of the same thing memoises on (position, last digit, started) and never on the tight state, since there is exactly one tight path.
hints: Group the numbers you are counting by the first position where they go below the bound. What is true of everything before that position, and what is free after it?
How many ways are there to fill k positions if each digit only has to differ from its neighbour on the left?
What happens to the prefix you are still following once the bound itself contains a repeat?
refs: LC 902 Numbers At Most N Given Digit Set

title: Who wins a multi-pile subtraction game
prompt: Write firstPlayerWins(piles []int, moves []int) bool. Two players alternate; a move removes exactly k stones from one pile for some k in moves, and a player with no legal move loses. Report whether the player to move wins under optimal play. moves holds distinct positive values, and the tests use up to 200000 piles of up to a million stones, so searching the combined game state is out.
explanation: The combined game has a state space that is the product of the pile sizes, so the only way through is to value each pile on its own and then combine. That is exactly what Sprague-Grundy gives you: every impartial game under normal play behaves like a single Nim pile whose size is its Grundy value, and the Grundy value of a position is the mex (minimum excludant) of the values of the positions reachable in one move. A pile of n here reaches n-k for each k in moves, so one linear pass over 0..maxPile fills the whole table, and each mex costs O(len(moves)). Combining is the part that is easy to get wrong: the value of independent games played side by side is the xor of their values, not the sum and not 'is any of them a win'. Two piles of 4 are each a win on their own, but together they are a loss, because the second player mirrors every move; xor gets that right and both of the plausible alternatives get it wrong. Zero means the player to move loses, so the answer is xor != 0. When the move set is 1..m the table collapses to n mod (m+1), which is the familiar special case, but the point of computing the mex is that it works for a move set with gaps too.
hints: The piles never interact, so what would you have to know about a single pile to be able to forget the rest of it?
For one pile, what is the smallest non-negative number that is not the value of any position you can move to, and why is that the right thing to record?
Two piles of equal size are always a loss. Which way of combining per-pile numbers has that property, and which two do not?

title: Count subsets under a bound with 40 numbers
prompt: Write countSubsetsAtMost(nums []int, target int) int returning how many of the 2^len(nums) subsets have a sum of at most target. The empty subset counts. The tests use 40 numbers of up to 10^12 each: 2^40 subsets is too many to enumerate, and the values are far too large for any table indexed by the sum.
explanation: Neither of the two usual attacks works here: enumerating 2^40 subsets is about 10^12 of them, and a knapsack table indexed by the sum would need 10^13 entries. What is left is to cut the input in half. Each half has only 2^20 subsets, about a million, which is cheap to enumerate outright. Then every subset of the whole is one subset of the left half plus one of the right, so the count you want is, summed over left sums a, the number of right sums b with b <= target - a. Sort both lists and that inner count is monotone: as a increases the allowed b shrinks, so a single pointer sweeping down the right list answers every query in O(1) amortised, and the whole thing is O(2^(n/2) * n) dominated by the sort. Binary searching per left sum is the same idea at O(2^(n/2) * n/2 * log) and is also fine. The rule of thumb worth carrying: n around 40 with no useful bound on the values is the signature of meet in the middle, because 2^(n/2) is a million and 2^n is not reachable. The recurring bug is the comparison boundary, since 'at most' has to include equality and duplicate values make many sums tie exactly on the target.
hints: 2^40 is out of reach but 2^20 is a million. What does that suggest doing to the input before you enumerate anything?
Once you have every sum from each half, what question do you have to ask the second list for each value in the first?
As the value from the first list grows, what happens to the answer to that question, and what does that let you avoid redoing?
